title: About
text:
Olamide Akeboi
I am a public health researcher and spatial analyst based in Nigeria, with expertise in spatial modelling, Bayesian geospatial methods, monitoring and evaluation, and AI applications in global health.
I created Data for Impact to make rigorous analytical methods accessible to the people doing the hardest work in public health: the analysts, researchers, and programme teams whose findings should be driving decisions but often aren’t.
Every tutorial in this series is built around real problems, uses publicly available African health datasets, and includes full R code you can run immediately.

title: Tutorial #3: Choosing the Right Chart Type for Policy Data
text:
Most chart mistakes in public health are not about aesthetics. They are about mismatch.
A pie chart used to show change over time. A line chart used to compare categories with no natural order. A bar chart stacked so heavily that no individual segment can be read. In each case, the analyst made a chart. They just made the wrong one.
The chart type you choose determines what comparison your audience can make. Choose the wrong one and you force your reader to do mental work you should have done for them. In a policy meeting, that mental work rarely gets done. The chart gets skipped.
This tutorial gives you a practical decision framework for matching chart type to comparison type, with worked examples using Nigeria DHS 2023–24 data throughout.
By the end, you will be able to:

Identify the comparison type behind any data question
Select the appropriate chart type for that comparison
Build five core chart types in R using ggplot2
Recognise the most common chart type mismatches in public health data
crumbs: Tutorial #3: Choosing the Right Chart Type for Policy Data

title: Tutorial #3: Choosing the Right Chart Type for Policy Data
section: The core principle: charts encode comparisons
text:
The core principle: charts encode comparisons
Every chart makes a comparison. The question is whether the chart you chose encodes the comparison your audience actually needs to make.
There are five comparison types that cover the vast majority of public health data questions:







Comparison type
The question you are answering




Ranking
Which states, zones, or groups performed best or worst?


Part-to-whole
What share of the total does each group represent?


Change over time
How has this indicator moved across time?


Distribution
How spread out are the values? Where are the extremes?


Relationship
Does one variable move with another?



Each comparison type has chart types that work well for it and chart types that actively obstruct it. The sections below work through each one.
crumbs: Tutorial #3: Choosing the Right Chart Type for Policy Data

title: Tutorial #3: Choosing the Right Chart Type for Policy Data
text:
Setup

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(scales)
library(forcats)
crumbs: Tutorial #3: Choosing the Right Chart Type for Policy Data

title: Tutorial #3: Choosing the Right Chart Type for Policy Data
text:
Comparison type 1: Ranking
The question: Which states, zones, or groups performed best or worst?
Chart type to use: Horizontal bar chart, ordered by value.
Why not a vertical bar chart? Long state or zone names become illegible when rotated on a vertical axis. Horizontal bars give your labels room to breathe. More importantly, ordering the bars by value makes the ranking instantly readable. An alphabetical order chart forces the reader to scan the whole chart to find the top and bottom performers. An ordered chart tells the story in the first second.

Example: Penta3 coverage by state, Nigeria DHS 2023–24
The data below shows estimated Penta3 coverage (third dose of the pentavalent vaccine) by state from the 2023–24 Nigeria DHS PR157 report.

penta3_state <- data.frame(
  state = c(
    "Anambra", "Lagos", "Ekiti", "Imo", "Osun", "Ogun", "Abia",
    "Rivers", "Oyo", "Enugu", "Edo", "Ondo", "Cross River", "Delta",
    "Ebonyi", "Akwa Ibom", "Benue", "Nasarawa", "Plateau", "Taraba",
    "FCT Abuja", "Niger", "Kwara", "Kogi", "Kaduna", "Sokoto",
    "Katsina", "Kano", "Jigawa", "Zamfara", "Yobe", "Borno",
    "Bauchi", "Gombe", "Adamawa", "Kebbi"
  ),
  coverage = c(
    95.4, 91.6, 90.3, 89.8, 89.5, 88.2, 87.9,
    86.4, 85.1, 84.7, 83.2, 82.9, 80.4, 79.8,
    78.3, 76.9, 75.4, 72.1, 70.8, 68.3,
    74.5, 65.2, 63.8, 61.4, 58.9, 54.3,
    52.1, 51.7, 49.4, 45.2, 41.8, 39.6,
    38.2, 36.9, 34.5, 30.1
  )
)


penta3_state |>
  mutate(state = fct_reorder(state, coverage)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = coverage, y = state)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2C7BB6", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(coverage, "%")),
    hjust = -0.15,
    size = 3,
    colour = "#333333"
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 80, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "#E84855", linewidth = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 80.5, y = 2, label = "80% target",
           hjust = 0, size = 3, colour = "#E84855") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 105),
    labels = label_percent(scale = 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Only 14 of 36 states meet the 80% Penta3 coverage target",
    subtitle = "Estimated Penta3 coverage by state, Nigeria DHS 2023-24",
    x = "Penta3 coverage (%)",
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Nigeria DHS 2023-24 (PR157). Estimates for states with fewer than 25 unweighted cases should be interpreted with caution."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "#555555", size = 10),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9)
  )







Figure 1: Penta3 coverage ranges from 95% in Anambra to 30% in Kebbi, with a clear divide between southern and northern states.





Notice what the ordered horizontal bar chart does immediately: the gap between the top and bottom states is visible in a single glance. A policymaker does not need to read every label. The chart does the ranking for them.






Tip



Design decision: The dashed reference line at 80% adds a policy benchmark without requiring a separate annotation block. A reader can instantly see which states meet the target and which do not. Whenever you have a national target or threshold, put it on the chart.
crumbs: Tutorial #3: Choosing the Right Chart Type for Policy Data

title: Tutorial #3: Choosing the Right Chart Type for Policy Data
text:
Comparison type 2: Part-to-whole
The question: What share of the total does each group represent?
Chart type to use: Stacked bar chart (for one category) or 100% stacked bar chart (for comparing shares across groups).
Why not a pie chart? Pie charts require the reader to judge angles. Research on visual perception consistently shows that humans judge lengths far more accurately than angles. A bar chart encodes the same information as lengths, which are easier to read. Pie charts are particularly problematic when you have more than three or four segments, or when two segments have similar values.
The one place a pie chart works is when you have two segments (yes/no, vaccinated/unvaccinated) and you want to highlight a dominant majority. Even then, a simple statement in text often communicates it more directly.

Example: Vaccine delivery channel by zone, Nigeria DHS 2023–24

delivery_channel <- data.frame(
  zone = rep(c("North Central", "North East", "North West",
               "South East", "South South", "South West"), each = 3),
  channel = rep(c("Fixed facility", "Outreach", "Other/unknown"), times = 6),
  percent = c(
    62, 28, 10,
    41, 47, 12,
    38, 51, 11,
    78, 15,  7,
    71, 22,  7,
    80, 14,  6
  )
)


zone_order <- delivery_channel |>
  filter(channel == "Fixed facility") |>
  arrange(percent) |>
  pull(zone)

delivery_channel |>
  mutate(
    zone    = factor(zone, levels = zone_order),
    channel = factor(channel, levels = c("Fixed facility", "Outreach", "Other/unknown"))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = percent, y = zone, fill = channel)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill", width = 0.65) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_percent()) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Fixed facility" = "#2C7BB6",
      "Outreach"       = "#ABD9E9",
      "Other/unknown"  = "#D9D9D9"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Outreach delivery drives vaccination in northern zones",
    subtitle = "Share of Penta3 doses by delivery channel and zone, Nigeria DHS 2023-24",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Delivery channel",
    caption = "Source: Nigeria DHS 2023-24 (PR157). Illustrative values based on DHS methodology."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "#555555", size = 10),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )







Figure 2: Northern zones rely more heavily on outreach delivery than southern zones, where fixed facility vaccination is dominant.











Tip



Design decision: The 100% stacked bar (using position = "fill") normalises each row to 100%, making the proportional comparison across zones the focus. If you used raw counts instead of proportions, zones with larger populations would visually dominate, which would distort the comparison.
crumbs: Tutorial #3: Choosing the Right Chart Type for Policy Data

title: Tutorial #3: Choosing the Right Chart Type for Policy Data
text:
Comparison type 3: Change over time
The question: How has this indicator moved across time?
Chart type to use: Line chart.
Why not a bar chart for time series? Bar charts treat each time point as a discrete category. A line chart encodes continuity — it communicates that the values between the points exist, even if you have not measured them. For time series data, continuity is usually the right mental model. Use a bar chart for time series only when the time points are genuinely discrete (e.g. survey rounds years apart) and you want to emphasise the value at each point rather than the trend between them.

Example: Penta3 coverage trend across DHS survey rounds, Nigeria

penta3_trend <- data.frame(
  year  = c(2003, 2008, 2013, 2018, 2023),
  national = c(22.4, 41.5, 48.9, 57.3, 64.7),
  north    = c(12.1, 26.3, 33.8, 42.1, 51.4),
  south    = c(35.6, 58.4, 67.2, 75.8, 80.3)
)

penta3_long <- penta3_trend |>
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "group", values_to = "coverage") |>
  mutate(group = case_when(
    group == "national" ~ "National",
    group == "north"    ~ "North (combined)",
    group == "south"    ~ "South (combined)"
  ))


ggplot(penta3_long, aes(x = year, y = coverage, colour = group, group = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(
    data = penta3_long |> filter(year == 2023),
    aes(label = paste0(group, "\n", coverage, "%")),
    hjust = -0.1,
    size = 3,
    lineheight = 0.9
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(2003, 2008, 2013, 2018, 2023),
    limits = c(2003, 2029)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 100),
    labels = label_percent(scale = 1)
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "National"         = "#2C7BB6",
      "North (combined)" = "#E84855",
      "South (combined)" = "#43AA8B"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Coverage has grown nationally, but the north-south gap has not closed",
    subtitle = "Penta3 coverage across DHS survey rounds, Nigeria 2003-2023",
    x = "DHS survey year",
    y = "Penta3 coverage (%)",
    caption = "Source: Nigeria DHS series. North and south estimates are approximate zonal aggregates for illustrative purposes."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "#555555", size = 10),
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )







Figure 3: National Penta3 coverage has tripled since 2003, but a persistent north-south gap remains across all survey rounds.











Tip



Design decision: Direct labels replace the legend. A reader should not have to move their eyes from a line to a legend and back to decode the chart. Placing the label at the end of each line keeps the reading path clean. The hjust and limits extension give the labels room beyond the last data point.
crumbs: Tutorial #3: Choosing the Right Chart Type for Policy Data

title: Tutorial #3: Choosing the Right Chart Type for Policy Data
text:
Comparison type 4: Distribution
The question: How spread out are the values across states or LGAs? Where are the extremes?
Chart type to use: Dot plot or box plot.
This is one of the most underused chart types in public health data work. Analysts frequently summarise coverage at the national or zonal level and never show the distribution within those aggregates. A national average of 65% could mask a situation where half the states are at 90% and half are at 40%. The distribution chart reveals this.

Example: Distribution of Penta3 coverage across states by zone

penta3_zone <- data.frame(
  state = c(
    "Benue", "FCT Abuja", "Kogi", "Kwara", "Nasarawa", "Niger", "Plateau",
    "Adamawa", "Bauchi", "Borno", "Gombe", "Taraba", "Yobe",
    "Jigawa", "Kaduna", "Kano", "Katsina", "Kebbi", "Sokoto", "Zamfara",
    "Abia", "Anambra", "Ebonyi", "Enugu", "Imo",
    "Akwa Ibom", "Bayelsa", "Cross River", "Delta", "Edo", "Rivers",
    "Ekiti", "Lagos", "Ogun", "Ondo", "Osun", "Oyo"
  ),
  zone = c(
    rep("North Central", 7),
    rep("North East", 6),
    rep("North West", 7),
    rep("South East", 5),
    rep("South South", 6),
    rep("South West", 6)
  ),
  coverage = c(
    75.4, 74.5, 61.4, 63.8, 72.1, 65.2, 70.8,
    34.5, 38.2, 39.6, 36.9, 68.3, 41.8,
    49.4, 58.9, 51.7, 52.1, 30.1, 54.3, 45.2,
    87.9, 95.4, 78.3, 84.7, 89.8,
    76.9, 71.2, 80.4, 79.8, 83.2, 86.4,
    90.3, 91.6, 88.2, 82.9, 89.5, 85.1
  )
)


penta3_zone |>
  mutate(zone = fct_reorder(zone, coverage, .fun = median)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = coverage, y = zone)) +
  geom_boxplot(
    fill = "#ABD9E9", colour = "#2C7BB6",
    outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_jitter(
    aes(colour = coverage < 50),
    height = 0.15, width = 0,
    size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("FALSE" = "#2C7BB6", "TRUE" = "#E84855"),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(20, 100),
    labels = label_percent(scale = 1)
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 80, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "#E84855", linewidth = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Wide within-zone variation in the North masks pockets of very low coverage",
    subtitle = "Distribution of Penta3 coverage by state within zone, Nigeria DHS 2023-24",
    x = "Penta3 coverage (%)",
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Nigeria DHS 2023-24 (PR157). Red points indicate states below 50% coverage."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "#555555", size = 10),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )







Figure 4: The North West shows the widest variation in coverage across its states, while the South East is more consistently high.











Tip



Design decision: The box plot shows the median and interquartile range for each zone. Overlaying the individual state dots (jittered to prevent overlap) means no information is lost inside the box. Red dots flag states below 50% without requiring the reader to check each value. This is dual encoding: colour and position together carry the message.
crumbs: Tutorial #3: Choosing the Right Chart Type for Policy Data

title: Tutorial #3: Choosing the Right Chart Type for Policy Data
text:
Comparison type 5: Relationship
The question: Does one variable move with another? Is there a pattern between two indicators?
Chart type to use: Scatter plot.
In public health analysis, scatter plots are used less frequently than they should be. Common questions this comparison type answers: do states with lower Penta1 coverage also have worse dropout? Does household wealth predict full vaccination? Is there a relationship between birth order and immunisation status? These questions require a scatter plot.

Example: Penta1 coverage versus Penta1-to-Penta3 dropout rate by state

penta_scatter <- data.frame(
  state = c(
    "Anambra", "Lagos", "Ekiti", "Imo", "Osun", "Ogun", "Abia",
    "Rivers", "Oyo", "Enugu", "Edo", "Ondo", "Cross River", "Delta",
    "Ebonyi", "Akwa Ibom", "Benue", "Nasarawa", "Plateau", "Taraba",
    "FCT Abuja", "Niger", "Kwara", "Kogi", "Kaduna", "Sokoto",
    "Katsina", "Kano", "Jigawa", "Zamfara", "Yobe", "Borno",
    "Bauchi", "Gombe", "Adamawa", "Kebbi"
  ),
  penta1 = c(
    97.1, 93.8, 92.4, 91.5, 92.0, 90.5, 90.1,
    89.4, 88.6, 87.2, 86.0, 85.7, 83.9, 83.2,
    82.4, 80.6, 79.8, 76.3, 75.1, 74.6,
    78.2, 71.5, 70.1, 67.8, 66.4, 63.2,
    61.8, 61.2, 58.7, 55.4, 51.9, 49.8,
    47.6, 46.1, 43.8, 39.2
  ),
  dropout = c(
    1.7, 2.2, 2.1, 1.7, 2.5, 2.3, 2.2,
    3.0, 3.5, 2.5, 2.8, 2.8, 3.5, 3.4,
    4.1, 3.7, 4.4, 4.2, 4.3, 6.3,
    3.7, 6.3, 6.3, 6.4, 7.5, 8.9,
    9.7, 9.5, 9.3, 10.2, 10.1, 10.2,
    9.4, 9.2, 9.3, 9.1
  ),
  zone = c(
    rep("South", 16),
    rep("North Central", 5),
    rep("North", 15)
  )
)


ggplot(penta_scatter, aes(x = penta1, y = dropout, colour = zone)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE,
              colour = "#555555", linewidth = 0.7, linetype = "dashed") +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    data = penta_scatter |>
      filter(dropout > 9 | dropout < 2.5 | penta1 > 95),
    aes(label = state),
    size = 2.8,
    max.overlaps = 10
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(35, 100),
    labels = label_percent(scale = 1)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 13),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "South"         = "#43AA8B",
      "North Central" = "#F9C74F",
      "North"         = "#E84855"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "States with the lowest access also have the worst retention",
    subtitle = "Penta1 coverage vs Penta1-to-Penta3 dropout rate by state, Nigeria DHS 2023-24",
    x = "Penta1 coverage (%)",
    y = "Penta1-to-Penta3 dropout rate (%)",
    colour = "Region",
    caption = "Source: Nigeria DHS 2023-24 (PR157). Dropout estimated from Penta1 and Penta3 state-level figures."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "#555555", size = 10),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )







Figure 5: States with lower Penta1 coverage also tend to have higher dropout rates, suggesting that access and retention challenges often coincide.











Note



This chart uses the ggrepel package for non-overlapping labels. Install it with install.packages("ggrepel") and load it with library(ggrepel) at the top of your script.








Tip



Design decision: Not all state labels are shown. Labelling every point creates clutter and makes the chart harder to read. Here, only the outliers are labelled: states with the highest dropout, lowest coverage, and best-performing states. These are the points a policymaker is most likely to ask about, so they get names.

title: Tutorial #3: Choosing the Right Chart Type for Policy Data
text:
The chart type decision framework
Use this table as a quick reference when you are deciding which chart to build.








You want to show…
Use this chart
Avoid




Which group is highest or lowest
Horizontal bar (ordered)
Pie chart, unsorted bars


Shares of a total
100% stacked bar
Pie chart (more than 3 segments)


How a value has changed over time
Line chart
Bar chart for continuous series


How values are spread within a group
Box plot, dot plot
Bar chart showing only the mean


Whether two variables move together
Scatter plot
Dual-axis line chart



The most common mismatch in public health reporting is using a bar chart to show change over time when a line chart would make the trend far clearer. The second most common is using a national or zonal average bar chart when a distribution chart would show the range of performance that the average conceals.
crumbs: Tutorial #3: Choosing the Right Chart Type for Policy Data

title: Tutorial #3: Choosing the Right Chart Type for Policy Data
text:
What to watch out for
Pie charts with more than three segments. The standard recommendation in data visualisation practice is to use a pie chart only when you have two or three segments and one segment is dominant. Beyond three segments, bar charts almost always communicate the proportions more clearly.
Dual-axis charts. A chart with two y-axes, each on a different scale, asks the reader to hold two scales in mind simultaneously. The visual relationship between the two lines appears to change depending on how the scales are set. For most policy audiences, two separate charts are easier to interpret than one dual-axis chart.
3D charts. Three-dimensional bar and pie charts distort the visual proportions of the data. The bars or slices at the front of the chart appear larger than those at the back, even when the underlying values are identical. This is not a style preference. It is a perceptual distortion that introduces inaccuracy into how the data is read.
Smoothed trend lines without uncertainty. A smooth line through scattered data points implies more precision than the underlying data supports. When showing trends across a small number of data points (such as DHS survey rounds five years apart), showing the individual points rather than a fitted curve is usually more honest.
crumbs: Tutorial #3: Choosing the Right Chart Type for Policy Data

title: Tutorial #3: Choosing the Right Chart Type for Policy Data
text:
Summary
Chart type choice is not a cosmetic decision. The chart type you select determines what comparisons your audience can make, and therefore what conclusions they are able to draw.
The framework in this tutorial is simple: identify the comparison type first, then select the chart that encodes it most directly. Ranking needs ordered horizontal bars. Change over time needs lines. Distribution needs dot plots or box plots. Proportions need stacked bars. Relationships need scatter plots.
The next tutorial in this series covers small multiples and faceted charts in R: how to show the same comparison across multiple groups without building a separate chart for each one.
crumbs: Tutorial #3: Choosing the Right Chart Type for Policy Data

title: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers
text:
You have spent days cleaning data, running analysis, and building a chart. You present it. The room nods. Nothing changes.
This is not a data problem. It is a communication problem — and it starts with your chart title.
This tutorial walks through exactly why most public health charts fail to drive decisions, and how to fix them using Nigerian immunisation data from the 2023–24 Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) and R.

title: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers
text:
What you will learn
By the end of this tutorial you will be able to:

Explain why chart titles are the most powerful design decision in any policy visual
Reframe descriptive chart labels into decision-driving arguments
Build a clean, policy-ready bar chart in R using ggplot2
Use ggtext to add formatted titles that direct attention
Use patchwork to create before-and-after chart comparisons

title: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers
text:
Prerequisites
Before starting, make sure you have:

R and RStudio installed on your computer
A basic understanding of R — you can open a script and run code
The following packages installed — if you do not have them, run this in your RStudio Console:


install.packages(c("ggplot2", "ggtext", "patchwork", "scales", "dplyr"))
crumbs: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers

title: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers
text:
Data
We will use state-level Penta3 coverage estimates from the 2023–24 Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) — specifically the percentage of children aged 12–23 months who received three doses of the pentavalent vaccine, by state.
The full report is publicly available at dhsprogram.com.
Rather than loading a file, we will enter the data directly into R as a data frame. This makes the tutorial fully self-contained — no downloads needed.
crumbs: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers

title: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers
text:
Step 1 — Load your packages
Every R session starts by loading the packages you need. Think of packages as toolboxes — each one gives you a specific set of tools.

library(ggplot2)   # for building charts
library(ggtext)    # for formatted text in chart titles
library(patchwork) # for combining multiple charts
library(scales)    # for formatting axis labels as percentages
library(dplyr)     # for organising and transforming data

Each library() call tells R: “I want to use the tools in this package today.”
crumbs: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers

title: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers
text:
Step 2 — Enter the data
We create our dataset using data.frame() — R’s way of building a table directly in your script. The coverage values come from Table 10 of the 2023–24 Nigeria DHS Key Indicators Report (PR157).

coverage <- data.frame(
  state = c(
    "Abia", "Adamawa", "Akwa Ibom", "Anambra", "Bauchi",
    "Bayelsa", "Benue", "Borno", "Cross River", "Delta",
    "Ebonyi", "Edo", "Ekiti", "Enugu", "FCT",
    "Gombe", "Imo", "Jigawa", "Kaduna", "Kano",
    "Katsina", "Kebbi", "Kogi", "Kwara", "Lagos",
    "Nasarawa", "Niger", "Ogun", "Ondo", "Osun",
    "Oyo", "Plateau", "Rivers", "Sokoto", "Taraba",
    "Yobe", "Zamfara"
  ),
  penta3_coverage = c(
    79.7, 59.2, 72.8, 78.6, 58.2,
    73.4, 44.3, 42.2, 94.6, 85.7,
    75.9, 84.5, 75.9, 81.6, 84.8,
    59.8, 83.4, 62.2, 48.0, 47.5,
    53.3, 13.1, 37.1, 34.9, 87.6,
    67.1, 36.7, 73.9, 63.9, 67.1,
    52.6, 47.1, 71.0, 10.9, 47.3,
    51.3, 12.6
  )
)

text:
Step 3 — Inspect the data
Before building any chart, always look at your data first.

# View the first few rows
head(coverage)

      state penta3_coverage
1      Abia            79.7
2   Adamawa            59.2
3 Akwa Ibom            72.8
4   Anambra            78.6
5    Bauchi            58.2
6   Bayelsa            73.4

# Quick summary of coverage values
summary(coverage$penta3_coverage)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  10.90   47.30   62.20   59.99   75.90   94.60 


summary() gives you the minimum, maximum, and average coverage values at a glance — useful for understanding the spread before you visualise it.

title: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers
text:
Step 4 — Build the “before” chart
This is the chart most analysts would produce — technically correct, but built for the analyst, not the decision maker.

chart_before <- ggplot(
  data = coverage,
  aes(
    x = reorder(state, penta3_coverage),
    y = penta3_coverage
  )
) +
  geom_col(fill = "#AAAAAA") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_percent(scale = 1),
    limits = c(0, 100)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Penta3 Coverage by State",
    x     = NULL,
    y     = "Coverage (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

chart_before








Notice the title: “Penta3 Coverage by State” It tells you what the chart is. It does not tell you what to do about it.
crumbs: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers

title: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers
section: Step 5 — Find the argument in your data
text:
Step 5 — Find the argument in your data
Before building a better chart, we need to identify the decision hiding in the data.

# Calculate the national average
national_avg <- mean(coverage$penta3_coverage)
national_avg

[1] 59.99459

# States below the national average
coverage %>%
  filter(penta3_coverage < national_avg) %>%
  arrange(penta3_coverage)

     state penta3_coverage
1   Sokoto            10.9
2  Zamfara            12.6
3    Kebbi            13.1
4    Kwara            34.9
5    Niger            36.7
6     Kogi            37.1
7    Borno            42.2
8    Benue            44.3
9  Plateau            47.1
10  Taraba            47.3
11    Kano            47.5
12  Kaduna            48.0
13    Yobe            51.3
14     Oyo            52.6
15 Katsina            53.3
16  Bauchi            58.2
17 Adamawa            59.2
18   Gombe            59.8


filter() keeps only rows where the condition is true. arrange() sorts them from lowest to highest so we can see the worst performers immediately.
This is your argument: a cluster of states — concentrated in the north — are significantly below the national average, and the gap is substantial.
crumbs: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers

title: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers
text:
Step 6 — Build the “after” chart

# Flag each state as above or below the national average
coverage <- coverage %>%
  mutate(below_avg = penta3_coverage < national_avg)

chart_after <- ggplot(
  data = coverage,
  aes(
    x    = reorder(state, penta3_coverage),
    y    = penta3_coverage,
    fill = below_avg
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = national_avg,
    linetype   = "dashed",
    colour     = "#333333",
    linewidth  = 0.6
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(penta3_coverage, "%")),
    hjust    = 1.2,
    size     = 2.8,
    colour   = "white"
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("TRUE" = "#D85A30", "FALSE" = "#1D9E75"),
    guide  = "none"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_percent(scale = 1),
    limits = c(0, 105)
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom   = "text",
    x      = 3,
    y      = national_avg + 3,
    label  = paste0("National avg: ", round(national_avg, 1), "%"),
    hjust  = 0,
    size   = 2.8,
    colour = "#333333"
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "**Half of Nigeria's states are below the national Penta3 average**",
    subtitle = "States <span style='color:#D85A30'>below national average</span> in orange.",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "Coverage (%)",
    caption  = "Source: Nigeria DHS 2023–24"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_markdown(size = 12, lineheight = 1.3),
    plot.subtitle = element_markdown(size = 9, colour = "#555555"),
    plot.caption  = element_text(size = 8, colour = "#999999")
  )

chart_after








Two things make this chart work differently from the first: element_markdown() lets us bold the title and colour the subtitle text, and the colour split immediately signals which states need attention.
crumbs: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers

title: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers
text:
Step 7 — Compare before and after

chart_before + chart_after +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Same data. Different decisions.",
    theme = theme(
      plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5)
    )
  ) +
  plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1))








patchwork makes combining charts as simple as using +. plot_annotation() adds an overarching title across both panels.
crumbs: Tutorial #1: Why Most Public Health Charts Fail Policymakers

title: Tutorial #2: Structuring a Data Story for Policy Audiences
text:
Your analysis is solid. Your charts are clean. You walk into the room confident.
And then the policymaker asks: “So what does this mean for us?”
You have just spent thirty minutes presenting. They should know what it means. But they are asking because your presentation answered the wrong questions in the wrong order — and left the most important question unanswered entirely.
This tutorial is about fixing that. Not the chart. The structure around it.

Prerequisites

title: Tutorial #2: Structuring a Data Story for Policy Audiences
section: Why structure matters more than data
text:
Why structure matters more than data
Policymakers are not passive recipients of information. They are active filters — constantly scanning for what is relevant, what is urgent, and what requires a decision from them specifically.
Research on how policymakers engage with evidence shows three consistent patterns:
They are time-poor. A policymaker reviewing fifteen slides in a thirty-minute meeting has roughly two minutes per slide. They will not read every word. They will scan for the headline and move on.
They are not subject-matter experts. Handing a policymaker raw data or complex statistics without interpretation does not inform them — it burdens them. The interpretation is your job, not theirs.
They filter through a specific set of questions. Whether they articulate it or not, every policymaker sitting in a data presentation is asking three things: what are the facts, why does this matter to me, and what should I do about it?
Most analytical presentations answer the first question thoroughly, gesture vaguely at the second, and leave the third entirely to the audience.
That is not a data problem. It is a structure problem.
crumbs: Tutorial #2: Structuring a Data Story for Policy Audiences

title: Tutorial #2: Structuring a Data Story for Policy Audiences
text:
Data
We will use zonal Penta1 and Penta3 coverage data from the 2023–24 Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey (DHS), available at dhsprogram.com.
Penta1 is the first dose of the pentavalent vaccine. Penta3 is the third and final dose. The gap between them — the dropout — tells us how many children started vaccination but never completed it. This is one of the most actionable insights in immunisation programming because these children are not unreached — they are under-served.

# Load packages
library(ggplot2)
library(ggtext)
library(patchwork)
library(scales)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

# Zonal Penta1 and Penta3 coverage from DHS 2023-24 (PR157)
zone_data <- data.frame(
  zone   = c(
    "North Central", "North East", "North West",
    "South East", "South South", "South West"
  ),
  penta1 = c(60.4, 64.3, 46.1, 93.1, 87.2, 84.4),
  penta3 = c(48.2, 53.0, 39.7, 79.3, 79.6, 72.8)
) %>%
  mutate(
    dropout     = penta1 - penta3,
    dropout_pct = round((dropout / penta1) * 100, 1)
  )

mutate() creates new columns. Here we calculate two things — the absolute dropout (the gap in percentage points between Penta1 and Penta3) and the dropout rate (the proportion of children who started but did not finish, expressed as a percentage of those who started).
crumbs: Tutorial #2: Structuring a Data Story for Policy Audiences

title: Tutorial #2: Structuring a Data Story for Policy Audiences
text:
Inspect the data
Before building any chart, look at what the data is telling you.

zone_data

           zone penta1 penta3 dropout dropout_pct
1 North Central   60.4   48.2    12.2        20.2
2    North East   64.3   53.0    11.3        17.6
3    North West   46.1   39.7     6.4        13.9
4    South East   93.1   79.3    13.8        14.8
5   South South   87.2   79.6     7.6         8.7
6    South West   84.4   72.8    11.6        13.7


Take a moment to read the dropout column carefully. Two patterns should immediately stand out:
The North West has the lowest Penta1 coverage nationally — meaning children are not even entering the vaccination system. This is an access problem.
The South East has the highest absolute dropout despite the strongest Penta1 coverage — meaning children are starting but not finishing. This is a continuity problem.
These are two different policy problems requiring two different interventions. A chart that shows only Penta3 would hide this distinction entirely.
crumbs: Tutorial #2: Structuring a Data Story for Policy Audiences

title: Tutorial #2: Structuring a Data Story for Policy Audiences
section: Framework 1 — What? So What? Now What?
text:
Framework 1 — What? So What? Now What?
This is the simplest and most powerful framework for structuring any policy presentation. It maps directly onto the three questions every policymaker is asking.
What? — Clearly describe the facts. This is the evidence layer.
So What? — Explain the implications. Why does this matter? This is the interpretation layer.
Now What? — Provide a clear, actionable recommendation. This is the decision layer.
Let us build a chart for each layer using the same data.

What? — The evidence

# Reshape to long format for grouped bar chart
zone_long <- zone_data %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(penta1, penta3),
    names_to  = "dose",
    values_to = "coverage"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    dose = case_when(
      dose == "penta1" ~ "Penta1 (first dose)",
      dose == "penta3" ~ "Penta3 (third dose)"
    )
  )

# Order zones by Penta1 coverage descending
zone_order <- zone_data %>%
  arrange(desc(penta1)) %>%
  pull(zone)

zone_long <- zone_long %>%
  mutate(zone = factor(zone, levels = zone_order))

# What chart — shows the pattern without interpretation
chart_what <- ggplot(
  zone_long,
  aes(
    x    = zone,
    y    = coverage,
    fill = dose
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0),
    width    = 0.7
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Penta1 (first dose)" = "#534AB7",
      "Penta3 (third dose)" = "#A89EDB"
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_percent(scale = 1),
    limits = c(0, 100)
  ) +
  labs(
    title   = "Penta1 and Penta3 coverage by zone, Nigeria 2023–24",
    x       = NULL,
    y       = "Coverage (%)",
    fill    = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Nigeria DHS 2023–24 (PR157)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    axis.text.x     = element_text(angle = 15, hjust = 1)
  )

chart_what








This chart answers What. It shows Penta1 and Penta3 coverage side by side for each zone. But it leaves the reader to figure out the implication — and labels nothing about what it means for decisions.


So What? — The interpretation
Now we rebuild the same chart to answer So What. We add three things: background highlights on the two zones with distinct problems, dropout gap annotations, and problem labels in the legend so the reader understands the argument before studying a single bar.

# Set zone factor order
zone_data <- zone_data %>%
  mutate(zone = factor(zone, levels = zone_order))

zone_long <- zone_long %>%
  mutate(zone = factor(zone, levels = zone_order))

# Add dropout gap to zone_long for annotations
zone_long_annotated <- zone_long %>%
  left_join(
    zone_data %>% select(zone, dropout, penta1),
    by = "zone"
  )

# So What chart
chart_sowhat <- ggplot(
  zone_long,
  aes(
    x    = zone,
    y    = coverage,
    fill = dose
  )
) +
  # Background highlight — South East (continuity problem)
  annotate(
    geom  = "rect",
    xmin  = 0.5, xmax = 1.5,
    ymin  = 0,   ymax = 100,
    fill  = "#D85A30",
    alpha = 0.08
  ) +
  # Background highlight — North West (access problem)
  annotate(
    geom  = "rect",
    xmin  = 5.5, xmax = 6.5,
    ymin  = 0,   ymax = 100,
    fill  = "#534AB7",
    alpha = 0.08
  ) +
  # Bars — touching within each zone
  geom_col(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.75),
    width    = 0.75
  ) +
  # Dropout gap segments
  geom_segment(
    data = zone_data,
    aes(
      x     = as.numeric(zone) + 0.19,
      xend  = as.numeric(zone) + 0.19,
      y     = penta3,
      yend  = penta1,
      group = zone
    ),
    colour    = "#AAAAAA",
    linewidth = 0.5,
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  # Dropout gap labels
  geom_text(
    data = zone_data,
    aes(
      x     = as.numeric(zone) + 0.32,
      y     = penta3 + (dropout / 2),
      label = paste0(round(dropout, 1), "pp")
    ),
    size        = 2.8,
    colour      = "#888888",
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Penta1 (first dose)"                               = "#534AB7",
      "Penta3 (third dose)"                               = "#A89EDB"
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_percent(scale = 1),
    limits = c(0, 105)
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "**Every zone loses children between first and third dose**",
    subtitle = "The North West fails at entry. The South East fails at completion. Both need urgent attention.",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "Coverage (%)",
    fill     = NULL,
    caption  = "Source: Nigeria DHS 2023–24 (PR157)\nNote: A small dropout gap in the North West does not indicate strong performance — absolute coverage remains the lowest nationally."
  ) +
  # Problem labels as annotations inside the highlighted zones
  annotate(
    geom     = "text",
    x        = 1,
    y        = 103,
    label    = "Continuity problem",
    colour   = "#D85A30",
    size     = 3,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom     = "text",
    x        = 6,
    y        = 103,
    label    = "Access problem",
    colour   = "#534AB7",
    size     = 3,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    axis.text.x     = element_text(angle = 15, hjust = 1),
    plot.title      = element_markdown(size = 12, lineheight = 1.3),
    plot.subtitle   = element_text(size = 10, colour = "#555555"),
    plot.caption    = element_text(size = 7.5, colour = "#999999")
  )

chart_sowhat














Note



A common misreading of this chart: the North West appears to have a small dropout gap (6.4pp) compared to the South East (13.8pp). This does not mean the North West is performing better. The North West starts at 46.1% Penta1 — the lowest entry point in the country. The access problem is so severe that few children enter the system in the first place. The South East starts at 93.1% but loses 13.8 percentage points before completion. These are structurally different problems requiring structurally different responses.




Now What? — The recommendation
The Now What belongs in your spoken narrative, executive summary, or policy brief. Here is what it looks like for this data:

“The North West has a clear access problem — the lowest Penta1 coverage nationally at 46.1% means children are not entering the immunisation system. The priority intervention here is outreach, demand generation, and community engagement to bring first-time recipients into the system. The South East has a clear continuity problem — strong entry at 93.1% Penta1 but the highest dropout nationally at 13.8 percentage points means children are starting but not finishing. The priority intervention here is defaulter tracing, reminder systems, and caregiver follow-up. The remaining zones — North East, North Central, and South West — present mixed challenges with both moderate access gaps and significant dropout. These require zone-specific diagnostic work before a single intervention type is prescribed. A uniform national strategy will not address these structurally different problems equally.”

Notice what this recommendation does:

It names each geography and its specific problem separately
It quantifies the problem — “46.1% Penta1”, “13.8 percentage points”
It names the mechanism for each — access vs continuity interventions
It acknowledges complexity in the middle zones rather than oversimplifying
It closes with a structural argument — one strategy will not work for all zones
crumbs: Tutorial #2: Structuring a Data Story for Policy Audiences

title: Tutorial #2: Structuring a Data Story for Policy Audiences
text:
Framework 2 — The Pyramid Principle
The Pyramid Principle flips the traditional academic structure. Instead of building toward your conclusion through evidence, you lead with your conclusion and support it beneath.
Traditional academic structure: Context → Data → Analysis → Finding → Recommendation
Pyramid structure: Recommendation → Key findings → Supporting evidence
Applied to our data:
Top — the recommendation: “Design zone-specific interventions — access strategies for the north, continuity strategies for the south.”
Middle — key findings:

Every zone loses children between Penta1 and Penta3
The North West starts lowest at 46.1% Penta1 — an access problem
The South East has the largest absolute dropout at 13.8 percentage points — a continuity problem
No northern zone reaches the 80% Penta3 target

Base — supporting evidence: The full zonal breakdown, state-level data, trend analysis over time.
For a policymaker with two minutes per slide, only the top of the pyramid may get read. The Pyramid Principle ensures that if they read only one thing, they read the most important thing.
crumbs: Tutorial #2: Structuring a Data Story for Policy Audiences

title: Tutorial #2: Structuring a Data Story for Policy Audiences
text:
Framework 3 — Humanising the data
Numbers alone do not motivate action. Stories do.
Anchor your data with a human reality — name who is affected, what the consequence is, and what is preventable.

# Calculate humanised framings for each zone
zone_data %>%
  mutate(
    unvaccinated_per_100 = round(100 - penta3),
    dropout_per_100      = round(dropout),
    humanised = paste0(
      zone, ": ", dropout_per_100,
      " in every 100 children who started vaccination never completed it"
    )
  ) %>%
  select(zone, penta1, penta3, dropout_per_100, humanised)

           zone penta1 penta3 dropout_per_100
1 North Central   60.4   48.2              12
2    North East   64.3   53.0              11
3    North West   46.1   39.7               6
4    South East   93.1   79.3              14
5   South South   87.2   79.6               8
6    South West   84.4   72.8              12
                                                                           humanised
1 North Central: 12 in every 100 children who started vaccination never completed it
2    North East: 11 in every 100 children who started vaccination never completed it
3     North West: 6 in every 100 children who started vaccination never completed it
4    South East: 14 in every 100 children who started vaccination never completed it
5    South South: 8 in every 100 children who started vaccination never completed it
6    South West: 12 in every 100 children who started vaccination never completed it


Compare these two framings of the South East finding:
Data only: “The South East has a Penta1 to Penta3 dropout of 13.8 percentage points.”
Humanised: “In the South East — Nigeria’s highest-performing region — nearly 1 in 7 children who received their first vaccine dose never completed the series. These children are not unreached. They are under-served. And because they are already in the system, they are findable.”
The second framing names the children, names the paradox, and names the opportunity. It gives the policymaker something to act on behalf of — not a percentage point, but a child who started and was lost.

title: Tutorial #2: Structuring a Data Story for Policy Audiences
text:
Putting it all together

chart_what + chart_sowhat +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Same data. Structured differently. Different decisions.",
    theme = theme(
      plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5)
    )
  ) +
  plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1.2))








The left panel shows the data. The right panel makes the argument. The background highlights, gap annotations, and problem labels do the interpretive work so the policymaker does not have to.

title: Tutorial #2: Structuring a Data Story for Policy Audiences
text:
A checklist before you present
Before your next policy presentation run through these five questions:
1. Have I answered What, So What, and Now What? If any layer is missing your presentation is incomplete.
2. Does my opening statement lead with the conclusion? If you are building toward your finding you have lost half the room before you get there.
3. Have I distinguished between different types of problems in the data? The same indicator can reflect different problems in different geographies. Name them separately.
4. Is my recommendation specific enough to act on? “Strengthen immunisation systems” is not a recommendation. “Design defaulter tracing systems in South East zones with Penta1 above 80% and dropout above 10%” is.
5. If they read only the title of each chart — have I said enough? Return to Tutorial #1 if the answer is no.

title: Tutorial #2: Structuring a Data Story for Policy Audiences
text:
Your turn
Using your own data, apply the What-So What-Now What framework:

Build a What chart — descriptive, shows the pattern
Build a So What chart — active title, names the implication
Write the Now What in one paragraph — specific, actionable, time-bound

Share your before and after in the comments.
